title: “DO YOU LOVE ME?”
paragraphs:
Not the fire of Pentecost.
Not yet.
This one crackled on a lonely shoreline in Gospel of John 21 — charcoal and smoke twisting into the morning air. The same smell as the courtyard.
Peter had gone back to fishing. Back to nets. Back to muscle memory. Because when shame screams loud enough, you return to what doesn’t ask questions.
But Jesus was waiting on the shore.
They don’t recognize Him. Not at first. The mist hangs low over the water. The sea is steel-blue. Their skin is wet with sweat and salt. Nets cutting into calloused hands. Empty.
“Cast the net on the right side.”
Fish thrashing silver in the rising sun. Water exploding in droplets. Nets straining. Hearts racing.
He doesn’t wait for the boat.
Why would a man who denied Jesus three times swim toward Him?
Because shame had one more round to lose.
On the shore: charcoal fire. Bread. Fish. Mercy in human form.
Jesus doesn’t start with the denial.
“Simon, son of John… do you love Me more than these?”
The same number as the denials.

Some scholars interpret the shift in Greek words for love (agape and phileo) as significant — others see it as stylistic. But the weight is undeniable. Jesus meets Peter exactly at the depth of his failure.

Each question peeling back pride. Each answer trembling.
“Yes, Lord… You know.”
By the third time, Peter is grieved.
Because godly sorrow is the doorway to restoration.

And then Jesus says it — not “Try harder.”
Not “Don’t mess up again.”

The same mouth that cursed and denied would preach at Pentecost.
The same hands that warmed by a coward’s fire would heal the lame.
The same heart that broke in shame would blaze in boldness.
But only if you turn back to the shore.

Not with words — but with silence.
With compromise.
With secret sin that smells like smoke.
And today Jesus stands on your shoreline.

Not “Are you perfect?”
Not “Did you get it right?”

Because love leads to repentance.
Repentance leads to restoration.
Restoration leads to purpose.
Peter’s story is not about a fisherman.

Jesus Christ died for deniers. He rose for failures. He restores the ashamed. At the cross, your worst moment met His greatest mercy. And in the resurrection, He calls you again — not to earn love, but to walk in it.
